q: Using the lot's total area and its frontage, what is the lot's depth, in meters?
n: Dividing the 200-square-meter lot area by its 10-meter frontage gives a depth of 20 meters.
scenario: A family has hired you as project architect for their upscale, two-storey single-detached residence within a gated subdivision in Makati City. Their interior lot totals 200 square meters, with a 10.00-meter frontage along a two-lane, two-way road right-of-way that runs along the lot's southern edge. Three-storey single-detached homes already stand on the neighboring lots to the west and east. The lot's northern edge borders a creek area governed by the easement rules of Presidential Decree 1067, and the ground slopes gently — about 2% — down toward that creek.

q: For this R-1 building type, the National Building Code requires a 4.50-meter front setback, the local ordinance requires 5 meters, and the subdivision's deed restrictions require 6 meters. Which of these governs?
n: When several regulations set different minimums for the same requirement, the most restrictive figure governs — here, the subdivision's 6-meter setback.

q: The National Building Code limits R-1 single-detached buildings to three storeys, but a local ordinance limits the same type to two storeys. Which limit controls?
o: Either applies equally, so it makes no difference
It is left to the Office of the Building Official to decide
n: Where a local ordinance imposes a stricter limit than the National Building Code, the stricter local standard controls — here, the two-storey cap.

q: Since the lot's rear edge borders the creek area, what must be legally provided or maintained along that boundary?
n: PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines) requires a mandatory easement along land bordering a creek, so an easement — not a promenade, esplanade, or the plain boundary line — applies here.

q: Because the site floods easily, the family patriarch — age 65 — wants the finished floor level raised 1 meter above natural grade, accessed by a single-flight ramp. Under Batas Pambansa Blg. 344, what horizontal run, in meters, must that ramp have?
ref: [Source: Batas Pambansa Blg. 344, as amended by the 2024 Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations, published in the Official Gazette, July 8, 2024 — Accessible Ramps, Sec. A.1.2 (Maximum Slope) and Sec. A.1.2(e) (Level Landing Requirement)]
n: Under the 2024 Revised IRR of BP 344, the maximum ramp slope is 1:20, with a steeper 1:15 exception allowed only for ramps with a maximum length of 10.50m and a maximum rise of 700mm. Since this ramp's rise is 1,000mm — above the 700mm cap — the 1:15 exception does not apply, and the ramp must follow the general 1:20 maximum slope. At 1:20, a 1-meter rise requires a 20-meter horizontal run. Adding the mandatory 1,800mm (1.8m) level landing at the ramp's upper end brings the total horizontal run to 21.8 meters.
